title: The UK constitution and its sources
subtitle: Why Britain writes its constitution nowhere in particular, and everywhere at once
objectives: Explain what it means to say the UK constitution is uncodified, and why 'unwritten' is a misleading label for it
Identify the four sources of the constitution — statute, common law, convention and prerogative — and place a given rule correctly among them
Explain what a constitutional statute is, why Thoburn gives it special legal weight, and apply that reasoning to a new example

leadingAuthorities.citation: Thoburn v Sunderland City Council [2002] EWHC 195 (Admin)
leadingAuthorities.role: Recognises a hierarchy of statutes: 'constitutional statutes' cannot be impliedly repealed

leadingAuthorities.citation: R (HS2 Action Alliance Ltd) v Secretary of State for Transport [2014] UKSC 3
leadingAuthorities.role: Confirms constitutional statutes and even more fundamental common law principles may limit how later statutes are read
Classic common-law source: state action requires positive legal authority
Early recognition that the Crown's prerogative is bounded by law, not self-defining

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students arrive able to say 'the UK doesn't have a written constitution' without being able to say what that actually means for a lawyer. This lesson replaces the slogan with a working toolkit: four sources, one hierarchy question, and a habit of asking 'where does this rule actually come from?'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You already know the four sources by name. What trips people up is sorting a new example correctly — is a Cabinet Manual rule a convention or codified practice? Expect the test pool to lean hard on classification.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and don't rush the four-source map in Part 2 — everything else in Public law assumes you can place a rule in the right box without hesitation.

overview.hook: Ask a hundred people where 'the British constitution' is kept, and most will say it doesn't exist. They're wrong, but understandably so — because unlike the United States, France or Germany, there is no single document you could point to, frame, and hang on a wall. The UK constitution lives in an Act of Parliament from 1215, a judge's ruling from last decade, an unwritten understanding about what the King will and won't do, and a convention nobody voted for but everybody obeys. This lesson is about finding it.

parts.heading: Uncodified, not unwritten
parts.voice: historical — traces how the absence of a founding document became the constitution's defining feature
body: Start by fixing the vocabulary, because loose language here costs marks. The UK constitution is not 'unwritten' — almost all of it is written down somewhere, in statutes, law reports and official documents. What it lacks is codification: there is no single, entrenched, foundational text that sits above ordinary law and that all other law must conform to, the way the US Constitution does.

This is a historical accident rather than a design choice. Most codified constitutions were written at a specific moment of rupture — independence, revolution, defeat, the founding of a new state. The UK has had no such single rupture since 1688, and even that Glorious Revolution produced a Bill of Rights that constrained the Crown without attempting to codify the whole system of government. Instead, the constitution accreted, statute by statute and case by case, over more than three centuries.

The practical consequence is that nothing in the UK constitution is legally entrenched in the way a codified constitution's core provisions typically are. In principle, Parliament could rewrite any constitutional rule with an ordinary Act, passed by simple majority, in an afternoon. Whether it actually could get away with that in practice — and what 'could' even means here — is the subject of Lesson 2. For now, hold onto the structural point: the UK constitution is a patchwork with no single frame, and lawyers have to know all four kinds of thread that go into it.

components.definition: A constitution not contained in a single authoritative document with special legal status; the UK's rules of government are instead scattered across statute, judicial decisions, convention and prerogative, with no formal hierarchy fixing one above the rest.

interaction.prompt: Which is the most accurate description of the UK constitution?
options: It is unwritten — almost none of it exists in documentary form
It is uncodified — its rules exist in writing but are scattered across multiple sources with no single foundational text
It does not exist as a legal matter, only as a political convention
interaction.trapExplanation: 'Unwritten' is the everyday phrase but the wrong one for exam purposes — most of the constitution is written, just not codified into one document. Calling it non-existent goes too far the other way: it produces real, enforceable legal rules, as the rest of this module will show.

parts.heading: Four sources, one map
parts.voice: structural — a reference part built for students to return to before exams
body: If the constitution isn't in one place, a public lawyer needs a reliable method for finding a given rule's source, because the source often determines the rule's legal force. There are four.

Statute is the strongest source in form, if not always in constitutional weight — an Act of Parliament, passed through the ordinary legislative process. Common law is judge-made: principles developed through case law, particularly around the rule of law and the limits of state power. Convention is a non-legal rule of political practice, binding by political and constitutional pressure rather than by court enforcement. Prerogative is the residue of the Crown's historic powers, now exercised almost entirely by ministers, and — as later lessons will show — shrinking every time Parliament puts a power onto a statutory footing instead.

Students often assume these four sources are ranked in a neat hierarchy. They are not, in the ordinary sense: a convention cannot be struck down by a court for conflicting with a statute, because a court has no jurisdiction to enforce a convention at all — but a statute can override or codify a convention outright, and frequently does. The safest approach is to treat the four as different in kind, not just in strength, and to ask two separate questions about any given rule: where does it come from, and who — if anyone — can enforce it?

components.label: The four sources of the UK constitution
points: Statute — an Act of Parliament; legally binding and enforceable in the ordinary courts
Common law — judge-made principle, developed through case law (e.g. the rule that state action needs positive legal authority)
Convention — a non-legal rule of political practice, binding by political pressure, not by courts
Prerogative — residual historic powers of the Crown, now almost always exercised by ministers, and displaceable by statute

components.factsShort: King's messengers ransacked Entick's home and papers under a warrant issued by the Secretary of State, with no statutory authority for the search.
components.ratioShort: State officials, like anyone else, can only act where the law positively permits it — there is no residual power to interfere with a subject's property simply because no law forbids it.

expanded.facts: John Entick's house was broken into and his papers seized on the authority of a general warrant issued by the Secretary of State, alleging seditious libel. No statute or established common law power authorised warrants of this general kind.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Camden CJ held that if the action could not be justified by law, it was a trespass, however senior the official who ordered it. The court rejected the argument that public officials could act as they pleased unless a specific law prohibited it.
expanded.significance: Entick is the foundation stone of the principle that the state has no power beyond what law grants it — the mirror image of the private citizen's freedom to do anything not prohibited. It remains the classic common-law source for the constitutional limits on executive action, cited as recently as the Miller litigation.

interaction.prompt: Tap the phrase in this sentence that identifies Entick v Carrington as a common law, rather than statutory, source of constitutional principle.
interaction.scenarioText: The court in Entick held that officials acting without any statutory warrant for their search had no lawful authority, a principle the judges derived from first principles about property and liberty rather than from any Act of Parliament.
tappableSpans: rather than from any Act of Parliament
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Exactly — the court reasoned the principle out for itself, which is what makes it common law rather than a rule enacted by Parliament.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the phrase describing where the judges got the rule from, not the phrase describing the facts of the case. The rule's origin — reasoned by judges, not enacted by Parliament — is what makes it common law.

parts.heading: Some statutes are more equal than others
parts.voice: case-narrative — builds the doctrine out of a genuinely odd set of facts about fruit and vegetables
body: Steve Thoburn sold bananas by the pound in his Sunderland greengrocer's, in defiance of metric-only regulations made under the European Communities Act 1972. He was prosecuted, and his defence raised a serious constitutional question: could the Weights and Measures Act 1985 — which he said still permitted imperial measures — have impliedly repealed the 1972 Act, on the ordinary rule that a later statute inconsistent with an earlier one repeals the earlier one by implication?

Laws LJ said no, and in doing so identified something new in English constitutional law: a category of 'constitutional statutes'. An ordinary statute can indeed be impliedly repealed by a later, inconsistent one — Parliament need not say 'I am repealing Act X' in so many words. But a constitutional statute — one that conditions the legal relationship between citizen and state, or that enlarges or diminishes fundamental constitutional rights — can only be repealed expressly, or by words so specific that repeal was unarguably intended.

This is a real, working legal doctrine, not just a label. Laws LJ listed examples: Magna Carta, the Bill of Rights 1689, the Act of Union, the Representation of the People Acts, the Human Rights Act 1998, the European Communities Act 1972 itself. The list is not closed, and later courts have added to the reasoning rather than the list — most notably in HS2, where the Supreme Court suggested some constitutional principles might sit at a level even statute cannot easily touch. Note precisely what the doctrine does and doesn't do: it does not entrench a constitutional statute against express repeal. Parliament remains free to repeal any of them outright, in clear words. What Thoburn removes is only the possibility of doing it by accident.

components.text: Subject to Schedule 2 to this Act, at any time after its passing, Her Majesty may by Order in Council, and any designated Minister or department may by regulations, make provision for the purpose of implementing any EU obligation of the United Kingdom...
elements: Delegated law-making power to implement EU obligations
Exercised by Order in Council or ministerial regulation
The Act itself later held to be a 'constitutional statute' in Thoburn

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often conclude that Thoburn means constitutional statutes can never be repealed, or that they sit permanently above ordinary Acts of Parliament.
components.whyItsWrong: Thoburn does not entrench constitutional statutes against Parliament's will — it only protects them from being repealed by accident, through the ordinary implied-repeal doctrine. Express repeal, in clear and specific words, remains entirely available to a later Parliament. The doctrine changes how repeal must happen, not whether it can.

interaction.prompt: Under Thoburn, can Parliament ever repeal a constitutional statute such as the Human Rights Act 1998?
options: No — constitutional statutes are permanently entrenched against repeal
Yes — but only by express words, not by a later inconsistent statute passed without mentioning it
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Thoburn only blocks implied repeal — accidental repeal by an inconsistent later Act. Parliament can still repeal a constitutional statute outright, in clear terms.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — Thoburn doesn't freeze constitutional statutes in place forever. It removes only the implied-repeal route; express repeal remains open to Parliament.

parts.heading: Convention: the rules nobody can sue over
parts.voice: dialectic — sets a puzzle (why obey a rule with no legal force?) and works through competing answers
body: Here's a puzzle worth sitting with. The monarch has, on paper, the legal power to refuse royal assent to any Bill passed by both Houses of Parliament. No statute forbids it. Yet no monarch has refused assent since Queen Anne in 1708, and it is universally accepted that a refusal today would be constitutionally impossible. What is stopping the monarch, if not law?

The answer is convention: a rule of political practice, observed because breaking it would be seen as illegitimate, not because a court would strike the breach down. Conventions govern huge swathes of how the UK is actually run — that the Prime Minister must command the confidence of the Commons, that ministers are collectively responsible for Cabinet decisions, that the Sewel Convention means Westminster will not normally legislate on devolved matters without the devolved legislature's consent.

Courts have repeatedly confirmed that conventions, however powerful in practice, are not law and cannot be enforced as such — that was the position taken toward the Sewel Convention when it was litigated in the first Miller case. But 'not law' doesn't mean 'not real'. Breaching a serious convention can end a government, force a resignation, or provoke a constitutional crisis far faster than breaching an ordinary statute would. The Ministerial Code, in this sense, functions more like an enforceable code of conduct sitting alongside conventions than a convention itself — it is a good example of how one 'source' category can shade into another, which is precisely why classification questions reward careful reading of the facts rather than a memorised label.

components.title: Is this rule law or convention?
components.description: A quick sorting test for a constitutional rule you encounter on the facts.

nodes.label: Would a court enforce this rule directly, striking down conduct that breaches it?
Yes → it is law (statute, common law, or a lawfully exercised prerogative power)
No → is it nonetheless treated as binding through political consequence (resignation, loss of confidence, crisis)?
No → it is likely a mere practice or preference, with no constitutional status at all

components.textAlternative: To classify a rule: first ask whether a court would enforce it directly. If yes, it is law. If no, ask whether it is nonetheless treated as binding through political consequence, such as forcing a resignation or a loss of confidence. If yes, it is a convention. If neither applies, it is likely just a practice or preference with no constitutional status.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a court could strike down a Prime Minister's decision purely for breaching the Sewel Convention?
interaction.explanation: Miller (No 1) confirmed that the Sewel Convention, however constitutionally significant, is not law and is not something the courts will police directly — its enforcement is political, through the relationship between Westminster and the devolved institutions, not judicial.

parts.heading: Prerogative: what's left of the Crown's own power
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the test pool will probe
body: The fourth source is the odd one out historically: the royal prerogative is what remains of the monarch's own inherent legal authority, once everything Parliament has since regulated by statute is subtracted. It is not granted by any document — it predates Parliament itself — but it is not unlimited either, and importantly, it is a residual category: it shrinks every time Parliament puts a power onto a statutory footing.

The Case of Proclamations settled the boundary early: the Crown cannot create new prerogative powers by proclamation, and cannot use the prerogative to change the law of the land or to create new offences — prerogative powers are recognised by courts as existing, not invented by the Crown at will. Today, prerogative powers are almost never exercised personally by the monarch; ministers exercise them in the Crown's name, covering matters like the conduct of foreign affairs, the deployment of the armed forces, and — until legislation intervened — the dissolution of Parliament.

Students often mistake 'prerogative' for 'unreviewable'. It is not: the extent and existence of a prerogative power is always a matter of law for the courts, and by the mid-1980s the courts had confirmed they can review how a prerogative power is exercised too, where the subject matter is justiciable. That story — and the two Miller cases that tested it against Brexit and against Parliament's own prorogation — is the subject of Lesson 6. For now, the point to fix is simpler: prerogative is a real, distinct source of constitutional authority, defined and bounded by the common law, not a blank cheque for the executive.

components.definition: The residual body of discretionary common law powers historically belonging to the Crown, now almost entirely exercised by ministers, whose existence and extent is a question of law for the courts and which is progressively displaced wherever Parliament legislates on the same ground.

interaction.prompt: Two scenarios describing government action with no statutory basis cited. Which most clearly involves the exercise of a prerogative power, rather than a claim to some other constitutional source?
interaction.scenarioA: A minister signs a treaty with a foreign state, relying on the Crown's historic power over foreign affairs, with no Act of Parliament authorising the specific treaty.
interaction.scenarioB: A minister announces that, by long-standing practice, the government will always resign if it loses a formal vote of no confidence in the Commons.
interaction.explanation: A is prerogative: the power to conduct foreign affairs and make treaties is a classic residual Crown power, exercised by ministers and grounded in no statute. B describes a convention — a rule of political practice with no legal source and no court enforcement, not a prerogative power at all.

testPool.prompt: Give the precise term for a constitution whose rules are written but scattered across multiple sources, with no single foundational document.
testPool.modelAnswer: Uncodified — the UK constitution's rules exist in writing, but are spread across statute, common law, convention and prerogative rather than gathered into one authoritative text.

testPool.prompt: Which case first recognised the category of 'constitutional statutes' protected from implied repeal?
options: Thoburn v Sunderland City Council
R (HS2 Action Alliance) v Secretary of State for Transport

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four recognised sources of the UK constitution?
options: Statute
Common law
Convention
Precedent set by the Cabinet Secretary
testPool.trapExplanation: Guidance from the Cabinet Secretary or the Cabinet Manual may record conventions, but it is not itself a fifth constitutional source — it is, at most, evidence of an existing convention or a codification of one, and its status is contested precisely because it fits awkwardly among the four established categories.

testPool.prompt: Which case established that state officials need positive legal authority for their actions, rather than merely acting where nothing forbids them?
options: Entick v Carrington
Case of Proclamations

testPool.prompt: Under Thoburn, what specifically distinguishes a constitutional statute from an ordinary one in terms of its legal effect?
options: A constitutional statute cannot be repealed by implication — only by express words or words unarguably intended to repeal it
A constitutional statute requires a two-thirds majority in the Commons to pass
A constitutional statute automatically overrides any later inconsistent statute, even an express repeal

testPool.prompt: In the passage below adapted from Thoburn, highlight the sentence that states the ratio on implied repeal of constitutional statutes.
testPool.passage: The Weights and Measures Act 1985 was said to impliedly repeal the European Communities Act 1972 so far as it permitted metric-only enforcement. Ordinary statutes may be impliedly repealed by later inconsistent ones, but constitutional statutes are not subject to implied repeal — the courts will only recognise repeal of a constitutional statute where the later statute expressly so provides, or where the wording is so specific that the intention to repeal is irresistible. On the facts, the 1985 Act did neither.
testPool.ratioSentence: constitutional statutes are not subject to implied repeal — the courts will only recognise repeal of a constitutional statute where the later statute expressly so provides, or where the wording is so specific that the intention to repeal is irresistible.

testPool.prompt: Put these steps of the Thoburn reasoning in the order the court took them.
items: Thoburn argues the 1985 Act impliedly repealed the metric-enforcement provisions of the 1972 Act
The court asks whether the 1972 Act is an ordinary statute or a constitutional statute
The court holds the 1972 Act is a constitutional statute, so implied repeal cannot apply
The 1985 Act is found not to expressly or unarguably repeal the 1972 Act, so the conviction stands

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that identifies this rule as a convention rather than a legal rule.
testPool.scenarioText: By long custom, a Prime Minister who loses a formal vote of no confidence resigns or seeks a dissolution; no statute compels this, but any Prime Minister who refused would face overwhelming political pressure to go, without any court having jurisdiction to order it.
testPool.explanation: The defining feature of a convention is not that it's old or that it's widely followed, but that no court can enforce it — its force is entirely political, not judicial.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario describes a prerogative power rather than a statutory one?
testPool.scenarioA: A minister grants planning permission under powers set out in the Town and Country Planning Act 1990.
testPool.scenarioB: A minister decides, without reference to any Act, to recognise a foreign government as legitimate.
testPool.explanation: Recognition of foreign governments is a classic prerogative power over foreign affairs, exercised by ministers with no statutory basis. A is exercised under an express statutory grant, so it is not prerogative at all.

testPool.prompt: Parliament passes a new Act that says nothing expressly about the Human Rights Act 1998 but contains provisions that are, in substance, inconsistent with several HRA sections. Applying Thoburn, has the HRA been repealed by implication?
options: Yes — inconsistency alone is always enough to repeal an earlier statute
No — as a constitutional statute, the HRA cannot be impliedly repealed by mere inconsistency; express words or unarguably specific wording are required
No — the HRA can never be repealed under any circumstances
testPool.explanation: This is Thoburn applied directly: mere inconsistency, without express repeal or unarguably specific wording aimed at the HRA, is not enough to repeal a constitutional statute. Parliament remains free to repeal it, but must do so clearly.

testPool.prompt: A minister exercises a power under an Act of Parliament that expressly covers the situation. A claimant argues the minister should instead have relied on an older prerogative power with looser conditions attached. Is the minister entitled to rely on the prerogative instead?
options: Yes — ministers may always choose whichever source of power is more convenient
No — once Parliament has legislated on a matter, the overlapping prerogative power is displaced and the statutory route must be used
Yes, provided the minister acted in good faith
testPool.explanation: This reflects the well-established principle (developed further in De Keyser's Royal Hotel, covered in Lesson 6) that statute displaces overlapping prerogative power — a minister cannot sidestep statutory conditions Parliament has imposed by falling back on an older prerogative covering the same ground.

testPool.prompt: A new Act of Parliament states, in a single unremarkable clause with no special mention of the ECA-derived constitutional framework, that 'all provisions of prior enactments inconsistent with this Act are repealed'. A litigant argues this silently repeals part of a constitutional statute. Analyse whether the argument succeeds.
factsToOrder: The clause is a general inconsistency-repeal clause
It does not name the constitutional statute or its provisions
The constitutional statute in question conditions the relationship between citizen and state
No express words or unarguably specific wording target the constitutional statute

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a general inconsistency-repeal clause in a later Act impliedly repeals part of an earlier constitutional statute.
modelAnswer.rule: Thoburn holds that constitutional statutes — those conditioning the relationship between citizen and state, or enlarging or diminishing fundamental rights — cannot be impliedly repealed; repeal requires express words or wording so specific that the intention to repeal is unarguable.
modelAnswer.application: The clause here is a generic inconsistency-repeal provision that does not name the constitutional statute or its provisions. Nothing about it is specific to the constitutional statute in question, so it falls well short of the 'unarguably intended' threshold Thoburn sets, however genuinely inconsistent the two Acts might be read to be.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The argument fails — the general clause is insufficient to repeal a constitutional statute; only express or unarguably specific words would do so.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best explains why conventions are described as constitutionally significant despite not being law?
options: Because breaching them, while lawful, typically carries severe political consequences that constrain behaviour as effectively as law does in practice
Because courts will fine ministers who breach them
Because conventions automatically become law once followed for a set number of years
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answers import legal enforcement mechanisms that simply don't exist for conventions — no fine, no automatic crystallisation into law. Their force is real but entirely political.

testPool.prompt: A litigant asks a court to declare that a minister acted unlawfully by breaching the Ministerial Code's rules on declaring conflicts of interest. Is a pure convention of this kind, standing alone, something a court will enforce directly?
options: No — a court will not enforce a convention as such, though the underlying conduct might separately engage reviewable legal duties
Yes — all conventions are directly enforceable exactly like statutes

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating 'constitutional' as a synonym for 'entrenched' or 'untouchable'. Thoburn only closes the accidental route (implied repeal) — Parliament's power to legislate expressly is never in doubt. Keep 'protected from implied repeal' and 'protected from repeal' strictly separate.
